 Inspiration 

 KHUM began with a frustrating experience inside a real clinic. 

 While helping the clinic set up an AI workflow, we discovered that its own customer, appointment, and operational data was locked inside a third-party ERP system. To let AI retrieve that data and reduce repetitive work, the clinic had to request API access from the software provider—and pay an additional fee—just to access data generated by its own business. 

 That experience revealed a much larger problem. 

 Businesses operate across ERPs, CRMs, property-management systems, spreadsheets, databases, email, messaging platforms, and many other applications. However, most of these systems were designed before AI agents and MCP became part of everyday work. 

 When a business wants its employees to work through AI, it faces a difficult choice: 

 
 Give employees access to sensitive API credentials. 
 Build a separate integration for every AI workflow. 
 Depend on software vendors to provide access. 
 Or allow AI to operate without sufficient control, visibility, and accountability. 
 

 We believe employees should be able to use the capabilities unlocked by business API connections without ever receiving, copying, or exposing the underlying API keys. 

 The business should remain in control of its data, permissions, budget, and actions. 

 That idea became KHUM . In Thai, “Khum” means to control . 

 What it does 

 KHUM is an industry-agnostic Business AI Control Plane that sits between AI agents, employees, and the software systems a business already uses. 

 An administrator connects the organization’s APIs, remote MCP servers, and databases to KHUM once. Credentials remain protected inside the platform and are never exposed to employees or AI clients. 

 The administrator can then create an Access Hub for any department, branch, team, project, or responsibility—for example: 

 
 Clinic Reception 
 Medical Operations 
 Finance 
 Hotel Front Office 
 Hotel Management 
 Sales 
 Human Resources 
 

 Each hub receives only the tools, systems, data fields, and actions required for its work. 

 Employees sign in using their own identities and interact through a compatible general-purpose AI agent. KHUM evaluates every request against the employee’s role, organizational scope, hub permissions, data policy, and budget before allowing it to reach an external system. 

 For read operations, KHUM returns only authorized information. 

 For actions that change data, send messages, create documents, or affect business operations, KHUM generates an exact preview and sends it through a human approval process before execution. 

 Every request produces an audit trail showing: 

 
 Who requested it 
 Which AI client initiated it 
 Which hub and business system were involved 
 What data was accessed 
 What action was proposed 
 Who approved or rejected it 
 What the final verified outcome was 
 How much the operation cost 
 

 On the web dashboard, KHUM uses WebMCP as the human–agent interaction layer. The page can dynamically expose only the tools available to the currently authenticated employee and their active hub. The browser agent can therefore perform structured operations inside the visible KHUM interface while the user retains context and control. 

 Behind that interface, KHUM connects to traditional REST APIs, OpenAPI services, remote MCP servers, and approved business databases. 

 In short, KHUM gives employees one governed AI interface while allowing the business to control every underlying connection. 

 How we built it 

 We started by mapping the real clinic workflow that inspired the project: where information was created, which third-party system stored it, who needed access, and where AI could reduce repetitive work. 

 From that workflow, we designed KHUM around five core layers: 

 
 Connection layer 
Connects business APIs, remote MCP servers, and approved database sources while keeping credentials on the server. 
 Identity and policy layer 
evaluates the organization, user, role, department, hub, requested tool, data scope, and budget for every operation. 
 WebMCP interaction layer 
exposes structured, context-aware tools to browser agents through the KHUM web interface instead of forcing agents to guess how to operate the UI. 
 Approval and execution layer 
converts sensitive write operations into immutable previews, routes them to authorized approvers, rechecks policy before execution, and verifies the result. 
 Audit and budget layer 
records access, actions, approvals, costs, errors, and uncertain outcomes in a searchable audit trail. 
 

 We designed logical MCP and WebMCP surfaces around each Access Hub. This allows one organization to support many departments without deploying and maintaining a separate physical server for every team. 

 We also created the first two industry packs: 

 
 Clinic Operations , focused on appointments, customer information, operational documents, and controlled communication. 
 Hotel Operations , focused on reservations, daily reporting, occupancy information, documents, and management summaries. 
 

 The current prototype validates KHUM’s product model, policy boundaries, approval lifecycle, data flows, and human–agent experience through an interactive architecture and workflow prototype. The next implementation milestone is a connector-backed pilot using synthetic data before introducing real customer credentials. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest challenge was not connecting APIs. It was deciding what should happen after they were connected. 

 A single shared integration must still produce different capabilities for different people. A receptionist, accountant, hotel manager, and business owner should not receive the same tools or see the same data simply because they belong to the same organization.
